content: AI agents differ from simple chatbots and deterministic workflows because they can use an iterative reasoning/action/observation process to decide runtime actions and tools toward a goal. Agents are most justified when paths are dynamic, inputs vary substantially, or tasks are long-horizon. Deterministic workflows remain preferable for predictable, auditable, high-volume, low-variance processes. Autonomy should be treated as a spectrum; greater autonomy requires stronger guardrails, evaluation, observability, and recovery.
key_concepts: chatbot responds without autonomous execution routing
agent can decide next actions/tools at runtime
deterministic workflows suit predictable fixed processes
simpler workflows reduce cost/latency for high-volume low-variance tasks
higher autonomy increases risk and control requirements

content: Task state is ephemeral and scoped to the current run, tracking progress and intermediate results. Memory persists beyond a task or session. Semantic memory captures stable facts or preferences, while episodic memory captures time-specific past events. Memory backends should match access patterns: summaries compress conversation, vector stores support semantic retrieval, and key-value stores support deterministic lookup. Good memory design is selective about what is written and retrieved and includes evaluation of memory usefulness.
key_concepts: memory persists beyond the current task/session
episodic memory stores time-specific past events
separate chat history from durable memory

topic: Agent Design Patterns and Multi-Agent Systems
content: Supervisor patterns coordinate and delegate to specialist agents, while reflection patterns alternate generation with critique and revision. Single agents can suffer context and prompt bloat and error contamination; multi-agent systems can separate responsibilities but add coordination risks. Planner–Executor separates planning from execution, while Router dispatches requests to an appropriate specialized path. Multi-agent systems can fail through duplicated work, cascading errors, and runaway loops, so handoffs and global execution limits require explicit controls.
key_concepts: reflection uses generation followed by critique/revision
single agents can suffer context/prompt bloat
router dispatches requests to appropriate specialized path

source.section: Agent Design Patterns and Multi-Agent Systems

content: Human-in-the-loop controls are important when agents can make consequential, customer-facing, irreversible, or low-confidence decisions. Approval checkpoints should be risk-based rather than applied to every output. High-confidence low-risk actions may proceed automatically, uncertain actions may require confirmation, and low-confidence or high-risk actions should stop or escalate. Review interfaces should expose enough evidence and task context for efficient decisions while avoiding reviewer fatigue.
key_concepts: human review reduces risk for consequential actions
review for low-confidence or sensitive outputs

content: Errors compound across long multi-step agent workflows, reducing end-to-end reliability. Cost controls include using smaller models for simple steps, caching, limiting retries and maximum steps, and avoiding unnecessary orchestration. Latency can be reduced by parallelizing independent calls, streaming, prefetching, and simplifying routing. Safe tool execution requires allowlists, strict input/schema validation, scoped permissions, risk-aware approval for writes, and sandboxing where appropriate.
key_concepts: per-step errors compound across multi-step tasks
longer task chains reduce end-to-end reliability
use smaller models for simple steps

content: The Agent Development Lifecycle progresses from scoping through prototyping/building, evaluation, deployment, and continuous monitoring/improvement. The MINT principle recommends starting with the simplest system that works and requiring each added layer of intelligence, tools, memory, or multi-agent orchestration to justify its cost, latency, security, and maintenance overhead. Evaluation should detect whether agents make meaningful progress and trigger bounded stopping, replanning, or escalation when progress stalls.
key_concepts: each complexity layer must justify its overhead
simpler deterministic or RAG workflow may be sufficient

content: MCP standardizes how AI applications connect to external tools, resources, and reusable prompts, reducing custom pairwise integration work. A2A addresses interoperability between agents rather than agent-to-tool connectivity. Interoperability expands attack surfaces, including malicious tool descriptions, injected tool output, over-scoped credentials, and unsafe writes; mitigations include vetting/version control, output handling, scoped short-lived credentials, and confirmation gates for destructive actions.
key_concepts: MCP standardizes connections between AI hosts and external capabilities
standard client/server interface reduces pairwise custom connectors
tool providers and clients implement the shared protocol
